title: Cultural, inclusive and social design

book.title: My Revision Notes: AQA A Level Design and Technology: Product Design

needs: Explain why products must be culturally acceptable, and what designers research.
Define inclusive design and give examples of it.
Give products that address social problems, poverty, health and wellbeing.
Describe how designers and organisations meet the needs of migrants, including housing.
Explain what Fairtrade is and what the Fairtrade mark shows.

doNow.q: Name two things designers research so a product is culturally acceptable.
doNow.a: How different genders see it; what its colour means in different countries; religious beliefs, traditions and customs.

doNow.q: What does the Fairtrade mark on a product show?
doNow.a: The product qualifies as Fairtrade: it is certified as fairly traded.

doNow.q: Give one thing Lego is doing as part of its corporate social responsibility.
doNow.a: Aiming for 100% renewable energy, only sustainable raw materials by 2030, or working with WWF to cut emissions.

doNow.q: What does the FSC scheme make sure of?
doNow.a: That timber is used sustainably: it comes from responsibly managed sources.

chunks.label: Cultural acceptability
chunks.summary: Products must not offend customers at home or abroad.

items.text: Products must not offend people in domestic or global markets.
Offended, alienated customers bring a financial cost and wider harm.
Research how different genders perceive the product.
A colour can mean different things in different countries.
Religious beliefs, traditions and customs may be outside the designer's experience.
Involve the communities concerned and avoid stereotypes or disrespectful symbols.

check.q: Why does offending customers matter to a business?
check.a: Offended, alienated customers bring a financial cost and other wider disadvantages.

check.q: Why must designers research the colour of a product before selling it abroad?
check.a: A colour can have a different cultural meaning in different countries.

chunks.label: Inclusive design
chunks.summary: Mainstream products that as many people as possible can use.

items.text: Mainstream products usable by as many people as possible without special adaptation (BSI).
items.caption: A diverse focus group helps designers understand different abilities, experiences and needs. Involving users early reduces assumptions and leads to more accessible products.

items.text: The DDA 1995, now replaced by the Equality Act 2010, changed public transport and access.
items.caption: Accessible transport demonstrates how design can remove physical barriers. Features such as low-floor buses and wheelchair ramps enable greater independence and equal access (now replaced by the Equality Act 2010).

items.text: Suit a diverse range of people without singling anyone out.
items.caption: OXO Good Grips uses ergonomic, easy-to-hold handles that benefit people with reduced grip strength. The products remain attractive and practical for everyone, avoiding stigma.

items.text: Wider doors for wheelchairs in new houses and OXO Good Grips easy-to-use utensils.
items.caption: Wider doorways and level thresholds accommodate wheelchair users, pushchairs and people with limited mobility. Designing accessibility into homes benefits a wide range of users.

items.text: Low-floor buses, bright-yellow handrails, crossings with bumps, ramps and sensory feedback.
items.caption: Low-floor buses, tactile paving and accessible crossings help people with different abilities navigate public spaces safely and independently.

items.text: In theatres, for audience members with a hearing impairment.
items.caption: Induction loops transmit sound directly to compatible hearing aids, reducing background noise. This improves accessibility in public places such as theatres and reception areas.

items.text: Kettle pourers and door handle adapters, sold by specialist shops.
items.caption: Kettle tippers reduce the strength and movement needed to pour hot water safely. Unlike universal products, specialist adaptations address particular user needs.

check.a: Designing mainstream products that as many people as reasonably possible can use, without special adaptation.

check.q: Give two examples of inclusive design on public transport or in the street.
check.a: Low-floor buses for wheelchairs, bright-yellow handrails, or crossings with raised bumps, ramps and sensory feedback.

chunks.label: Social problems
chunks.summary: Products whose design and manufacture tackle social issues.

items.text: Issues affecting people: environment, health, poverty, discrimination, unemployment.
items.caption: Designers can address problems such as pollution, poverty and poor health through innovative products and systems that improve behaviour, accessibility or living conditions.

items.text: Innovative bin designs encourage children to adopt good habits.
items.caption: Bright colours and playful animal shapes make disposing of litter more appealing to children. This shows how aesthetics can influence behaviour and encourage positive habits.

items.text: Car insurance companies use them to monitor young drivers.
items.caption: Telematics devices monitor driving behaviour, including speed and braking. Feedback and insurance incentives can encourage safer driving, particularly among young or inexperienced drivers.

items.text: Detect illegal drugs and explosives.
items.caption: Portable scanners help police identify potentially dangerous substances in the field. Their design prioritises accuracy, portability, durability and ease of use.

items.text: Solutions must not rely on resources or maintenance that aren't available locally.
items.caption: Manual water pumps demonstrate appropriate technology designed around local infrastructure and resources. Long-term success also depends on affordable maintenance, spare parts and available skills.

check.a: Issues affecting people, such as the environment, health, poverty, discrimination and unemployment.

check.q: Give one product designed to address a social issue.
check.a: Child-friendly litter bins, black box devices for young drivers, or police scanners for drugs and explosives.

chunks.label: Poverty, health and wellbeing
chunks.summary: Designers responding to the right to an adequate standard of living.

items.text: Everyone's right to food, clothing, housing and medical care for health and well-being.
items.caption: The UN recognises access to food, shelter and healthcare as basic human rights. Designers can contribute by developing affordable solutions that improve living standards.

items.text: A radio needing no batteries, by Trevor Baylis, for parts of Africa short of them.
items.caption: Trevor Baylis's radio converts stored mechanical energy into electricity. It provides access to information without relying on disposable batteries or mains electricity.

items.text: LED lighting replacing dangerous, costly kerosene lamps in Kenya.
items.caption: GravityLight generates electricity as a raised weight slowly descends. This innovative approach provides LED lighting without disposable batteries or fuel-burning kerosene lamps.

items.text: An NGO giving appropriate, technological 'open design' answers to poverty.
items.caption: Practical Action promotes appropriate technology designed around local needs. Successful solutions must be affordable, easy to use and maintainable using available resources.

items.text: A robotic surgery system by Intuitive Surgical, for advanced, safe surgery.
items.caption: The da Vinci system translates a surgeon's movements into precise robotic actions. Advanced control systems and articulated instruments enhance dexterity during minimally invasive surgery.

items.text: Improved prostheses using advanced composites, motors and control systems.
items.caption: The i-limb combines sensors, electronic controls and independently powered fingers. These technologies enable different gripping functions, improving independence for people with limb differences.

items.text: The NHS uses 3D printed polymer implants to repair skull injuries.
items.caption: Medical imaging and CAD enable patient-specific implants to match individual anatomy. Additive manufacturing can produce complex shapes that are difficult to manufacture conventionally.

check.q: What problem did the wind-up radio solve?
check.a: A lack of radio batteries in parts of Africa: it needs no batteries.

check.q: How does the NHS use 3D printing to improve health?
check.a: It makes 3D printed polymer implants to repair skull injuries.

chunks.label: Migration
chunks.summary: Meeting the basic needs of destitute migrants.

items.text: Conflict, poverty and victimisation leave huge communities of destitute migrants.
items.caption: Conflict and displacement create urgent demand for shelter, clean water and sanitation. Designers must develop affordable, portable solutions that can be deployed rapidly.

items.text: Provide basic infrastructure for these temporary communities.
items.caption: Organisations such as Oxfam and UNHCR provide essential infrastructure during humanitarian emergencies. Product solutions must be reliable, practical and suitable for challenging conditions.

items.text: From the UNHCR, for preparing food.
items.caption: Solar cookers concentrate or capture sunlight to heat food without conventional fuels. They can reduce fuel costs and firewood collection where sunlight is sufficient.

items.text: Technology from SunDwater, for clean water.
items.caption: Solar distillation uses heat to evaporate water before condensing the vapour into freshwater. It demonstrates how renewable energy can support access to clean water.

items.text: Multi-purpose clothing by Angela Luna that becomes a shelter.
items.caption: Angela Luna's ADIFF designs transform clothing into temporary shelters. This multifunctional approach combines portability, protection and adaptability to address the needs of displaced people.

items.text: Adapted shipping containers for medical care, from the UNFPA.
items.caption: Modified shipping containers provide transportable medical facilities. Their modular construction enables healthcare services to be deployed in areas lacking permanent infrastructure.

check.q: Why do humanitarian organisations need to provide basic infrastructure?
check.a: Conflict, poverty and victimisation create huge temporary communities of destitute migrants.
Shipping containers adapted to give medical care, from the UNFPA.

items.text: One of the key needs in a refugee crisis.
items.caption: Emergency shelters must balance safety, comfort, privacy and affordability. Lightweight, transportable designs help humanitarian organisations respond quickly to housing shortages.

items.text: The Ikea Foundation's flat-pack shelter, made to meet that need.
items.caption: Supported by the IKEA Foundation, Better Shelter applies flat-pack and modular design principles to emergency accommodation. Prefabricated components make transportation and assembly more efficient.

items.text: It can be put up without any tools.
items.caption: The shelter's modular construction reduces the need for specialist tools and building skills. This makes assembly more practical where resources and trained workers are limited.

items.text: Each shelter sleeps five people.
items.caption: Better Shelter provides approximately 17.5 m² of internal space for five people. Its design balances essential living space with material efficiency and transportability.

items.text: The shelter is well insulated.
items.caption: Lightweight wall and roof panels provide greater protection from the elements than basic emergency tents. Material choice and ventilation influence comfort, durability and thermal performance.

items.text: A solar-powered electrical system.
items.caption: An integrated solar-powered lighting system provides illumination without relying on mains electricity. This improves usability and independence in locations with limited infrastructure.

check.q: Who made the flat-pack Better Shelter?
Give three features of the Better Shelter.
check.a: Put up without tools, sleeps five, well insulated, solar-powered electrical system.

chunks.label: Fairtrade
chunks.summary: Ethical treatment of farmers and workers in developing countries.

items.text: A movement for the ethical treatment of farmers and workers in developing countries.
items.caption: Fairtrade promotes better trading conditions for farmers and workers. Ethical design considers working conditions, fair treatment and the social impact of manufacturing decisions.

items.text: The Fairtrade organisation negotiates fair prices with buyers.
items.caption: Fairtrade Minimum Prices provide a safety net for eligible producers when market prices fall. An additional Fairtrade Premium supports investment in businesses and communities.

items.text: A certification label shown on qualifying products.
items.caption: The FAIRTRADE Mark identifies products meeting recognised certification standards. It allows consumers to make informed choices and helps brands communicate ethical sourcing.

items.text: A UK fair trade pioneer that sold ethically sourced products until administration in January 2023.
items.caption: Traidcraft pioneered fair trade in the UK by creating markets for ethically sourced products. It demonstrated how responsible purchasing can support producers and communities.

items.text: Schools and councils seek it to promote sustainable development, producer benefits, active citizenship and demand.
items.caption: Schools and councils can promote Fairtrade through purchasing policies and awareness campaigns. These initiatives encourage ethical consumption and help increase demand for responsibly sourced products.

items.text: A Fairtrade organisation in India giving craftspeople sustainable work and social benefits.
items.caption: Pushpanjali supports Indian craftspeople through the production and sale of handmade goods. Fair trading relationships help preserve traditional skills while supporting employment and livelihoods.

items.text: Shoppers recognise the scheme, so it affects material choice, branding and demand.
items.caption: Ethical considerations influence material selection, manufacturing, supply chains and packaging. Fairtrade certification can also strengthen a product's branding and appeal to socially conscious consumers.

check.q: What does the Fairtrade organisation do for producers?
check.a: Negotiates fair prices for their products with buyers.

check.q: Why might a school seek Fairtrade status?
check.a: To promote sustainable development, benefits for producers, active citizenship and demand for Fairtrade food and craft.

quiz.q: Why must companies avoid creating offensive products?
options: Offended customers bring a financial cost and other disadvantages
They can't carry the Fairtrade mark
quiz.why: Alienating customers costs the business money and causes wider problems.

quiz.q: The colour of a product can have a different cultural meaning in different countries.
quiz.why: Designers research what colours mean in each country they sell to.

quiz.q: Designers only need to think about the culture of their home market.
quiz.why: Products must be acceptable in global markets as well as domestic ones.

quiz.q: Which organisation's definition of inclusive design is used?
quiz.why: The British Standards Institution (BSI) defines inclusive design.

quiz.q: Inclusive design means making a special adapted version of a product for each user.
quiz.why: It means mainstream products usable by as many people as possible without special adaptation.

quiz.q: Which 1995 law, now replaced by the Equality Act 2010, affected public transport and access?
options: The Copyright, Designs and Patents Act
quiz.why: The DDA 1995 made an impact on public transport and access. The Equality Act 2010 has now replaced it.

quiz.q: In England, Scotland and Wales the Equality Act 2010 replaced the DDA 1995.
quiz.why: The Equality Act 2010 now protects disabled people from discrimination.

quiz.q: Who do hearing induction loops in theatres help?
options: Audience members with a hearing impairment
quiz.why: Induction loops are for audience members with a hearing impairment.

quiz.q: OXO's Good Grips range is an example of inclusive design.
quiz.why: The award-winning range of kitchen utensils is designed to be easy to use.

quiz.q: Which is a social issue?

quiz.q: Why do car insurance companies use 'black box' devices?
quiz.why: The device monitors how young drivers drive.

quiz.q: A solution to a social problem should rely on maintenance that isn't available locally.
quiz.why: Designers must understand the local context and avoid solutions that depend on unavailable resources or maintenance.

quiz.q: Which right does Article 25 of the UN Declaration of Human Rights (1948) give everyone?

quiz.why: It includes food, clothing, housing and medical care.

quiz.q: How many people does a Better Shelter sleep?

quiz.q: What does the Fairtrade organisation negotiate with buyers?
quiz.why: It secures fair prices so farmers and workers are treated ethically.

quiz.q: Schools and local authorities can seek Fairtrade status.
quiz.why: They do it to promote sustainable development, producer benefits, active citizenship and demand.

quiz.q: Where is the Fairtrade organisation Pushpanjali?
quiz.why: Pushpanjali gives craftspeople in India sustainable work and social benefits.

quiz.why: Traidcraft plc, a UK fair trade pioneer, went into administration in January 2023.

written.q: A company is about to sell a new product in several countries. Explain why its designers must consider cultural acceptability.
points: Offensive products offend and alienate potential customers…
…which brings a financial cost and wider disadvantages for the business.
A colour can have a different cultural meaning in different countries.
Different genders may see the product differently.
Religious beliefs, traditions and customs may be outside the designer's own experience…
…so they need research, involving people from those communities.
written.model: If the product offends people, customers are alienated, which brings a financial cost and wider disadvantages for the business. The designers need to research what its colours mean in each country, because a colour can mean different things in different places. Religious beliefs, traditions and customs may be outside their own experience, so they should involve people from those communities in their research.
written.note: 1 mark per point or explanation, up to 4.

written.q: Describe two examples of inclusive design and who each one helps.
points: Wider doors in new houses…
…so wheelchair users can get through.
Low-floor buses…
…so wheelchair users can get on.
Hearing induction loops in theatres…
…for audience members with a hearing impairment.
OXO Good Grips kitchen utensils…
…easy to use for as many people as possible.
written.model: Hearing induction loops are fitted in theatres, so audience members with a hearing impairment can follow the performance. Low-floor buses let wheelchair users get on without needing a special vehicle.
written.note: 1 mark for each example and 1 for who it helps, up to 4.

written.q: Explain two ways designers and organisations have met the needs of migrants in temporary communities.
points: The UNHCR's solar cookers…
…meet the need for food preparation.
SunDwater's water distillation technology…
…meets the need for clean water.
Angela Luna's Adiff multi-purpose clothing…
…meets the need for clothing and can become a shelter.
The Ikea Foundation's flat-pack Better Shelter…
…meets the need for temporary accommodation.
The UNFPA's hospitainers and maternitainers…
…adapted shipping containers that give medical care.
written.model: The UNHCR provides solar cookers, which meet the need for food preparation in temporary communities. The Ikea Foundation designed the flat-pack Better Shelter to meet the need for temporary accommodation: it can be put up without tools and sleeps five people.
written.note: 1 mark for each example and 1 for explaining the need it meets, up to 4.

written.q: Compare the wind-up radio and the GravityLight as design responses to poverty.
points: Both remove the need for supplies that are scarce or costly.
Both avoid relying on resources that aren't available locally.
The wind-up radio needs no batteries; the GravityLight replaces kerosene lamps.
The radio tackled a lack of batteries in parts of Africa; the light tackles the danger and expense of kerosene in Kenya.
The radio was by Trevor Baylis; the light by the GravityLight Foundation.
written.model: Both designs remove the need for supplies that are scarce or costly, so they don't rely on resources that aren't available locally. The wind-up radio needs no batteries, which tackled a lack of batteries in parts of Africa, while the GravityLight gives LED lighting to replace dangerous, expensive kerosene lamps in Kenya.
written.note: 1 mark per valid comparison point, up to 4.

written.q: Evaluate how far inclusive design can meet the needs of every user of an everyday product such as a kettle.
points: Inclusive design aims for mainstream products usable by as many people as reasonably possible.
Users don't need special adaptation, so no one is stigmatised.
It considers differences in age, strength, dexterity, reach, vision, hearing, cognition and mobility.
Examples such as OXO Good Grips show everyday products can be easy to use for more people.
It doesn't mean every product suits every person: the designer defines the user group and reduces the main barriers.
Some people still need specialist products, such as kettle pourers from specialist shops.
Justified conclusion, e.g. it can meet most users' needs, but specialist products are still needed for some.
written.model: Inclusive design aims to make mainstream products, such as a kettle, usable by as many people as reasonably possible, without special adaptation, so no one is stigmatised. It considers differences in age, strength, dexterity, reach, vision and mobility, and products like OXO Good Grips show that everyday items can be easy for more people to use. However, it doesn't mean every product can suit every person: the designer defines a user group and reduces the main barriers, so some people still need specialist products such as kettle pourers. Inclusive design can meet most users' needs, but not everyone's, so specialist products are still needed.

levels.text: Detailed, balanced points on both sides, with a justified conclusion.
Some points, mostly on one side, or a conclusion that isn't justified.

written.note: Tick the points made, then use the levels under the model answer to decide the mark.

written.q: Explain what the Fairtrade mark on a product tells a shopper.
points: The product is certified as qualifying for Fairtrade…
…so the farmers and workers in developing countries who made it were treated ethically and paid a fair price.
written.model: The Fairtrade mark is a certification label showing the product qualifies as Fairtrade, so the farmers and workers in developing countries who produced it were treated ethically and paid a fair price.
written.note: 1 mark for the point, 1 for explaining it.
